definition: The product that results from the complete acidulation and thorough settling of soapstock. Contract grade should contain not less than 85% total fatty acid.
Bleaching earth that has been treated with acid to increase its capacity for pigment adsorption from oil.

Chief components and determinants of the characteristics of a protein; the building blocks of living tissues. Eighteen different amino acids commonly occur in our food supply and eight are considered essential because the body cannot produce them.

Any naturally occurring or manufactured material whose incorporation into a fat provides a greater stability than that shown by the fat alone. The antioxidant increases stability by preventing or retarding reaction of the fat with oxygen and thus retards rancidity development. Antioxidants for food fats must be nontoxic and edible.
See Methyl esters

The science of using living things, such as plants or animals to develop new products or make modifications to existing ones. Current methods include the transfer of a gene from one organism to another. Also see "Genetic engineering," and "Transgenic."

Treatment of a fat or oil with a material such as activated charcoal or diatomaceous (Fullers) earth which removes or reduces the amount of coloring materials normally present in a refined oil. The bleaching process may be carried to the degree desired depending upon the color required by the eventual usage of the processed oil.
Mined special earths or clays that when added to hot oil, at about 1%, have the ability to adsorb unwanted pigments.
The pods or capsules of certain plants, especially flax or cotton.
A class of soybean trypsin inhibitors that has low molecular weight, many disulfide links, and great stability to denaturation.
Pericarp of grain.

Flocculent material (precipitate) that appears in and can be separated from crude vegetable oil that has been rapidly heated to temperatures between 250°C and 300°C (482°F and 572°F). It is very high in ash content, rich in phosphorus, calcium and magnesium. It is presumed to be derived from phospholipids which are thermally decomposed at these high temperatures. Break material is sometimes referred to as "foots."
The mass resulting from the pressing of seeds, meat, or fish in order to remove oils, fats, or other liquids.

The seed of the species Brassica napus or Brassica campestris, the oil component of which seed contains less than two percent of erucic acid and the solid component of which seed contains less than 30 micromoles of any one or any mixture of 3-butenyl glucosinolate, 4-pentenyl glucosinolate, 2-hydroxy-3-butenyl glucosinolate, and 2-hydroxy-4-pentenyl glucosinolate per gram of air dry, oil free solid. The term is derived from combining the words "Canadian" and "oil" and is a registered trademark of the Canola Council of Canada.

Consists of the meal obtained after the removal of most of the oil, by a direct solvent or prepress solvent extraction process, from the whole seeds of the species Brassica napus or Brassica campestris (see Canola, above).

Any material which speeds up a chemical reaction without taking part directly in the chemical changes involved. The presence of a catalyst may be desirable as in the hardening and stabilizing of an oil by chemical addition of hydrogen in the presence of nickel catalyst.

Fruit of the Cocos nucifera. Consists of mesocarp (fibrous covering), endocarp (shell), exocarp (the smooth outer skin) and copra meat or flesh. Husked coconut has outer layers removed. Immature nuts contain an edible milky juice. Mature nuts are consumed as such, or processed for copra or desiccated coconut. The flesh, from which coconut oil is extracted, constitutes 40-70% of the weight of the husked coconut. The oil content is about 36% of the flesh.
See Copra meal

The liquid found inside a coconut is coconut water. Coconut milk is a liquid extracted from the grated white flesh of the coconut. The fat rich layer that forms on the top of thick coconut milk after a couple of hours in the refrigerator is coconut cream.
Dried, shredded flesh of coconut processed for human consumption. It retains most of the oil and proteins of the fresh nut and is mainly used in confectionery and baking.
Soy oil produced from undamaged, mature, cleaned yellow soybeans by mechanical processing and filtering, without the application of heat.

A test which determines how well the high melting point portions of an oil have been removed during processing to produce a "salad" or "winterized" oil. In the test the oil sample is held in an ice water bath (32°F) and the time required for the first appearance of cloudiness is noted.
Also known as non-oil or edible sunflower (Helianthus annuus L.). Includes seed for human consumption and bird food.

A refined, bleached, and deodorized oil which has not been further processed to remove the higher melting point portions of the oil. Cooking oils tend to crystallize or set up semisolid at temperatures much below about 70°F.
The dried flesh of coconut from which the oil is extracted.
The ground residue which remains after removal of most of the oil from dried meat of coconuts by either mechanical or solvent extraction process.
The outer coating of the corn kernel, with little or none of the starchy part of germ.
The fine siftings obtained from screened cracked corn, with or without its aspiration products added.
The fine sized hard flinty portions of ground corn containing little or none of the bran or germ.
Ground corn germ from which most of the solubles have been removed by steeping and most of the oil removed by mechanical extraction processes.

The part of the commercial shelled corn that remains after the extraction of the larger portion of the starch, gluten, and by the processes employed in the wet milling manufacture of corn starch or syrup.
The dried residue from corn after removal of the larger part of the starch and germ, and the separation of the bran.
The medium sized hard flinty portions of ground corn containing little or none of the bran or germ.
The residue from the ginning of cotton. It consists of cotton burrs, leaves, stems, lint, immature seeds, and sand and/or dirt.
The unground product composed of the kernel and such portions of the lint, hull, and oil as remain after removal of most of the oil from cottonseed by a mechanical process.
Product obtained by finely grinding the cake which remains after removal of most of the oil from the cottonseed by a solvent extraction process.
The outer covering of the cottonseed.
Product obtained by finely grinding the cake which remains after removal of most of the oil from the cottonseed by a mechanical extraction process.
Obtained in the commercial delinting and processing of cottonseeds for planting purposes. It consists of lint, stems, leaves, small and immature seeds, sand and/or dirt.
Glandless cottonseed is the seed of cotton which has been selected through plant breeding to eliminate, or reduce to the extent practicable, seed pigment glands.
One of the two halves of a seed; the cotyledons develop into the first two leaves of the young plant.
The entire corn kernel ground or chopped. It must contain not more than 4% foreign material.
The breaking of the whole seed into several pieces to facilitate dehulling and flaking.
Crude cottonseed oil is the oil produced from cottonseed only, by either the hydraulic, expeller or screw press, prepress solvent, or solvent extraction process.
Sometimes referred to as crude raw soybean oil; the unrefined oil produced by any one of the procedures described for the extraction of oil from soybeans.
Flour produced by the nearly complete removal of the oil from soybeans by the use of hexane or other homologous hydrocarbon solvents; usually contains about 1% fat.
Having had the embryo of seeds wholly or partially separated from the starch endosperm.
The product resulting from washing crude soy oil with water and/or steam or another degumming agent for a specified period of time.
The removal of phospholipids from vegetable oil by a water washing step.
Having removed the outer covering from grains or other seeds.
A process involving use of high vacuum and superheated steam in washing of fats and oils to remove objectionable flavors and odors.
Equipment for removing solvent from defatted flakes and for heating flakes sufficiently to overcome growth inhibition properties.
A chemical combination of fatty acids and glycerine in the proportion of two fatty acid units to one glycerine unit.
An oil which is very easily oxidized and polymerized on exposure to air or oxygen. Used to fix or set pigments, as in paints.
Soy oil produced from mature yellow soybeans through various pressing or solvent extraction methods.
A material capable of causing fat or oils to remain in liquid suspension.
Starchy portion of seed.
The process of combining by chemical reaction an alcohol and an acid. The new product is an ester.
Subjected to moisture, pressure, and temperature to gelatinize the starch portion.
Equipment for expressing oil from oilseeds, consisting of an augur moving through a slotted barrel. Also called a continuous screw press.
Having removed fat or oil from materials by heat and mechanical pressure.
Having removed fat or oil from materials by organic solvents.
A process by which feed has been pressed, pushed, or protruded through orifices under pressure.
A jacketed augur used as an economical cooker and as a means of texturizing soy flours or other foodstuffs.
A process for texturizing soy flours or other proteins using high pressures and temperatures in an extruder.
A substance composed chiefly of triglycerides of fatty acids, and solid or plastic at room temperature.
A chemical unit occurring naturally, consisting of strongly linked carbon and hydrogen atoms in a chain-like structure.
Suitable for animal consumption.
Acted upon by yeasts, molds, or bacteria in a controlled aerobic or anaerobic process.
A process for converting typically dehulled oilseeds into thin flakes for solvent extraction or other processing.
Soft, finely ground and bolted meal obtained from the milling of cereal grains, other seeds, or products.
The amount of fatty acid, occurring naturally or produced in fat processing, which exists in the fat or oil in the uncombined state.
Ground whole soybeans containing all of the original oil usually 18 to 20%.
The edible oil produced from crude or degummed soy oil which has been neutralized, bleached, and deodorized.
The general process of transferring DNA from one organism to another to determine desirable traits.
The embryo found in seeds and frequently separated from the bran and starch endosperm during the milling.
A phenolic pigment in cottonseed that is toxic to some animals.
Seed from cereal plants.
Edamame (Japanese) Vegetable-type soybeans picked green and cooked until tender.
Coarsely ground grain from which the bran and germ have been removed.
Formation and accumulation of a fat-insoluble sticky material resulting from continued heating of fats and oils.
Soy flour produced by adding soy oil to defatted soy flour to a desired level, usually 10 to 20%.
A morphological feature of a seed coat; the point of attachment of the seed to the pod.
Outer covering of grain or other seed.
Vegetable oil exposed to hydrogen gas in the presence of heat and a catalyst to increase the melting point; "hardening."
The process of chemically adding hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst to stabilize and retard rancidity.
The product resulting from complete hydrolysis of isolated corn gluten.
Made from soybean flours, concentrates or isolates, treated with an acid, base, or enzyme and then dried.
Complex molecules having been split to simpler units by chemical reaction with water.
A subclass of flavonoids found in soybeans (genistein and daidzein) that may exert biological effects including cancer inhibition.
Soy protein concentrated to at least 90% by removing non-protein components.
Product obtained by cooking ground solvent extracted soybean meal under pressure and extruding it.
A class of soybean trypsin inhibitors believed to be primarily responsible for growth inhibition from raw soybeans.
The mixed phospholipids obtained from vegetable oils (soy, etc.) during the degumming process.
A type of soy flour in which lecithin is added to defatted soy flour, usually up to 15%.
Obtained by grinding the cake or chips remaining after removing oil from flaxseed.
The residual fibers removed from cottonseed by mechanical processes.
An iron-containing enzyme in soybeans primarily responsible for creating the "beany" flavor in soymilk.
Cottonseed meal in which the gossypol is not more than 0.04% free gossypol.
Flour produced either by partial removal of oil or by adding oil/lecithin back to defatted soy flour (5-6% fat).
Purified concentrated aqueous solution of nutritive saccharides derived from starch.
A water-in-oil emulsion used as a butter alternative.
Division of seed cultivars into 12 groups based on how flowering responds to dark periods.
Material prepared from vegetable protein to resemble specific meats in texture, color, and flavor.
Use of soy or other vegetable proteins as partial substitutes for meat in processed items.
The temperature at which a natural or processed fat becomes liquid.
Product of the reaction of fats with methyl alcohol; used as biodiesel fuel.
A fermented Japanese seasoning paste made from soybeans and microorganisms like Aspergillus oryzae.
A chemical compound of one fatty acid unit with one glycerine unit; used as an emulsifier.
A whole soybean product produced by fermenting cooked soybeans with Bacillus natto.
Foods containing naturally occurring compounds beneficial for disease treatment or prevention.
A substance composed chiefly of triglycerides of fatty acids and liquid at room temperature.
Soybean pulp remaining after the production of soymilk.
Oil produced from crude soy oil which has been subjected only to the alkali refining treatment.
Chemical reaction involving oxygen that results in rancidity in fats.
Oil obtained from the kernel of the oil palm fruit; similar to coconut oil.
Oil derived from the mesocarp of the fruit of the oil palm.
The liquid, more unsaturated fraction separated from palm oil after crystallization.
The more saturated and solid fraction obtained by fractionation of palm oil.
The outer hull of the peanut shell.
The ground product of shelled peanuts after oil extraction.
The outer covering of the peanut kernel, exclusive of the hull.
Agglomerated feed formed by compacting and forcing through die openings.
Undesirable clumping of fat units into larger insoluble units during frying.
A naturally occurring combination of amino acids containing nitrogen.
Annual leguminous crops yielding 1 to 12 grains or seeds within a pod (e.g., dry peas, beans).
A soluble trisaccharide found in soybeans responsible for flatulence.
Stage in fat oxidation characterized by sharp, acrid off-flavors.
Obtained by grinding the cake remaining after mechanical extraction of rapeseed.
Treatment of fat with caustic soda and water to remove impurities.
Numerical expression of the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in the substance.
A refined, bleached and deodorized edible oil that has been winterized to remain clear at low temperatures.
A plastic or semisolid fat used in bakery products to make them tender.
By-product from the alkali refining of vegetable oil.
A product from which oil has been removed by solvents (usually hexane).
Finely powdered material after removal of most oil from soybeans; < 4% fiber.
Granular material after removal of most oil from soybeans; < 4% fiber.
Contains not less than 65% protein on a moisture-free basis.
The major proteinaceous fraction of soybeans; contains not less than 90% protein.
A seasoning sauce of soybeans (and sometimes wheat) resulting from fermentation or acid hydrolysis.
Whole soybeans that have been sprouted (germinated) for up to six days.
Term describing the entire plant or crop (Glycine max).
Product resulting from extraction of oil from soybeans by pressure or solvents.
Outer covering of the soybean.
Ground soybean cake/flakes; standard 44% protein or high 48% protein versions.
Composed of soybean hulls and offal from the tail of the mill.
Whole soybeans heated without removing any component parts.
A legume (Glycine max); contains 18-22% oil and 38-45% protein.
Term for edible soy-based products (tofu, soymilk, tempeh, etc.).
Protein-rich milk-like liquid obtained from whole soybeans and water.
Roasted whole soybeans.
A soluble tetrasaccharide found in soybeans responsible for flatulence.
Obtained by grinding residue after solvent extraction of whole sunflower seed.
Indonesian soyfood made by fermenting cooked soybeans with Rhizopus oryzae.
Curds resulting from the coagulation of soymilk protein.
A plant or animal modified by genetic engineering to contain DNA from an external source.
The reaction product of one unit of glycerine with three units of fatty acid.
Ether soluble material extractable after reaction with strong alkali.
Refers to a shortage of hydrogen atoms in the oil structure; leads to higher reactivity.
A 100% vegetable fat blend of palm oil formulated as a butter replacement.
Oil chilled to remove high-melting-point saturated glycerides to remain clear when refrigerated.
Film formed by simmering soymilk, then lifting and dried.
